Class BoundedDataKeyStrategy

java.lang.Object
org.jwcarman.codec.crypto.BoundedDataKeyStrategy
All Implemented Interfaces:
DataKeyStrategy
public final class BoundedDataKeyStrategy extends Object implements DataKeyStrategy
Opt-in DataKeyStrategy that caches a data-encryption key (DEK) and rolls to a fresh one after maxMessages messages or maxAge has elapsed, whichever comes first.

Choosing a message cap

The message cap is validated to the range [1, 2^24]. At the 2^24 ceiling, the probability of a random-nonce collision under a single cached DEK is roughly 2^-49 — still well clear of the 2^32-random-nonce limit documented in NIST SP 800-38D for a single key, but this class deliberately refuses to be configured all the way up to that cliff edge. The recommended value is 2^20 (roughly 2^-57 collision probability), which is a comfortable margin for the vast majority of consumers. A consumer who genuinely needs a larger cap than 2^24 allows should implement the DataKeyStrategy SPI directly — that SPI exists precisely so this shipped class does not have to compromise on where it draws the line.

The cap counts messages, not bytes. The assumption behind that choice is that message sizes stay well below GCM's 64 GiB per-invocation plaintext limit; consumers encrypting exceptionally large messages under a shared DEK should account for that limit themselves.

Duration

Elapsed time is measured against a monotonic ticker injected as a LongSupplier of nanoseconds. The production default is System.nanoTime(); a deterministic ticker may be supplied for testing.

VM snapshot / clone caveat

In environments where a running VM or container may be snapshotted and cloned (e.g. certain serverless or sandboxed execution platforms), a clone can resume with an identical cached DEK and duplicated SecureRandom state, which can cause nonces to repeat under that shared key. DirectDataKeyStrategy does not remove the hazard when the data key comes from JceDataKeyProvider, whose DEK is drawn from the same cloned RNG: both clones then produce the same key and the same nonce. The mitigations are a KMS-backed provider (DEK entropy from outside the process), reseeding or replacing the SecureRandom and rolling this strategy's key on resume, or a platform that reseeds on VM-generation change.

One provider per cached key

The cached DEK is tied to the DataKeyProvider instance that issued it. If a strategy instance is shared between codecs built on different providers, an acquire from the other provider rolls rather than reusing a DEK wrapped under a KEK that provider does not hold. Sharing is still not recommended — each codec gets the amortisation it expects only with its own strategy — but it cannot produce undecodable output.

Key retirement

A retired DEK is simply released to the garbage collector when this strategy stops referencing it — there is no destroy() call and no close hook. SecretKeySpec as shipped by OpenJDK does not implement key destruction, and destroying a key that another thread may still be using to encrypt would be a use-after-destroy race. In-flight operations that already hold a retired DataKey remain valid; they are simply not handed out for new messages.

Concurrency and rolling

Bounds are enforced with atomics rather than a lock held for the whole check-and-decrement. Under contention, a roll may therefore happen one message earlier than strictly necessary, but it is never late: no thread can observe more than maxMessages successful uses of a single cached key. If the provider fails while rolling, the failure propagates to the caller and the expired or exhausted key is never reused.
